n: Luke tells us the point before the story: keep praying and don’t lose heart, even when answers seem slow.

f.g: Lose heart, give up.

n: A judge in some town had no reverence for God and no concern for people — the worst kind of person to hold power.

f.g: Respected, cared about.

n: A widow — among the most vulnerable people in that society — keeps coming to him, demanding justice against someone who has wronged her.

f.g: Widows often had no legal advocate; the law commanded special care for them.
Give me justice; vindicate me.

n: For a while he refuses. But eventually he admits to himself that, though he cares nothing for God or anyone...

f.g: In private reasoning — Luke often lets us hear characters’ thoughts.

n: ...this widow is wearing him out. He’ll give her justice just to get rid of her before she exhausts him.

f.g: Literally “give me a black eye” — wear me down.

n: Jesus says: listen to what even this unjust judge concluded.

f.g: The judge is a contrast to God, not a picture of Him.

n: If an unjust judge eventually helps, won’t a righteous and loving God help His own people who cry out to Him day and night? His timing may seem long, but He cares.

f.g: God’s chosen, covenant people.

f.w: though he bear long with them

n: God will bring justice, and when it comes it will be swift. The real question is whether Christ will find people still faithfully praying when He returns.

f.w: shall he find faith on the earth?

n: The next parable is aimed at people who were sure of their own goodness and looked down on everyone else.

f.g: Looked down on with contempt.

n: Two men go up to the temple to pray: a Pharisee, admired for strict observance, and a tax collector, despised as a collaborator and cheat.

f.g: A tax collector for Rome.
The temple sat on a hill, so worshippers always “went up.”

n: The Pharisee stands and prays “with himself” — really to himself. He thanks God that he isn’t like other people, including that tax collector over there.

f.g: Swindlers, people who rob by force or fraud.
Possibly “prayed to himself” — his prayer is self-focused.

n: He lists his religious achievements, going beyond what the law required. His prayer asks for nothing because he thinks he needs nothing.

f.w: I fast twice in the week
f.g: The law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement; devout Pharisees fasted Mondays and Thursdays.

n: The tax collector stands at a distance, won’t even look up, and beats his chest in sorrow. His prayer is just: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.

f.g: Beat his chest — a gesture of deep grief and remorse.

f.w: God be merciful to me a sinner
f.g: The Greek suggests “make atonement for me.”

n: Jesus declares that the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified — right with God. The humble are lifted up; the proud are brought down.

f.g: Declared righteous, put right with God.

f.w: he that humbleth himself shall be exalted

n: Parents bring even babies for Jesus to bless, but the disciples try to stop them, thinking He is too busy for children.

f.g: Greek brephē — babies.

n: Jesus calls the children to Him. God’s kingdom belongs to those who are like them — humble, trusting, and teachable.

f.w: Suffer little children to come unto me

f.g: Allow, let.

n: Anyone who doesn’t receive the kingdom with a child’s trust and humility will not enter it.
A ruler asks the great question: what must I do to inherit eternal life? He seems sincere but thinks of it as something to earn.

f.g: A leader — Matthew says he was young; all three Gospels say he was rich.

n: Jesus asks why he calls Him good, since only God is good. He is inviting the man to think about who Jesus really is.
Jesus lists commandments about how we treat others, from the Ten Commandments.
The ruler says he has kept them all since he was young. He may well have, outwardly.

f.g: Since boyhood.

n: Jesus sees what holds him back: he still lacks one thing. Sell everything, give to the poor, and follow Me. The invitation is to discipleship, not just a donation.
He becomes deeply sad, because he is extremely rich. His wealth had a stronger hold on him than he realized.

f.g: Grieved, distressed.

n: Seeing his sorrow, Jesus remarks how hard it is for the wealthy to enter God’s kingdom.

f.g: With what difficulty.

n: It’s easier for a camel — the largest animal in the region — to pass through a needle’s eye. The image is deliberately impossible.

f.w: a camel to go through a needle's eye
f.g: A vivid exaggeration typical of Jewish teaching; the popular “narrow gate” explanation is a later idea.

n: The hearers are stunned. Many saw wealth as a sign of God’s favor. If the rich can’t be saved, who can?

f.g: Their surprise reveals their assumption that riches meant blessing.

n: What is impossible for humans is possible for God. Salvation is always His gift, for rich and poor alike.
Peter points out that the disciples have left everything to follow Him.
Jesus assures them that anyone who has given up home or family for God’s kingdom...

f.w: for the kingdom of God's sake
f.g: For the sake of God’s work, not for selfish reasons.

n: ...will receive much more in this life and eternal life in the world to come. No sacrifice for God goes unrewarded.

f.g: Many times as much.

n: Taking the Twelve aside, Jesus tells them again that in Jerusalem everything the prophets wrote about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.

f.w: all things that are written by the prophets

n: He will be handed over to the Romans, mocked, insulted, and spit upon. This is His most detailed prediction of His suffering.

f.g: Treated with insolence and abuse.

n: They will flog Him and kill Him, but on the third day He will rise again. The Resurrection is always part of His prediction.

f.g: Flog with a whip — a brutal Roman punishment.

f.w: the third day he shall rise again

n: The Twelve don’t understand any of it. The meaning is hidden from them until after the Resurrection.

f.w: this saying was hid from them

n: Near Jericho, a blind man sits by the road begging. Mark names him Bartimaeus.

f.g: An ancient oasis city near the Jordan, about 17 miles northeast of Jerusalem.

n: Hearing a crowd passing, he asks what’s happening.

f.g: What was going on.

n: They tell him Jesus of Nazareth is passing by — perhaps his only chance.

f.g: A common way to identify Him by His hometown.

n: He cries out, calling Jesus “Son of David” — a messianic title. Though blind, he sees who Jesus really is.

f.g: A title for the promised Messiah, descended from King David.

n: People at the front scold him to be quiet, but he shouts all the louder. His persistence is the kind of prayer Jesus praised at the start of this chapter.

f.g: Be quiet.

n: Jesus stops — the whole procession halts for a single beggar — and has him brought over.

f.g: He stopped walking.

n: Jesus asks what he wants. The answer seems obvious, but Jesus invites him to express his faith and desire.

f.w: What wilt thou that I shall do unto thee?

n: Jesus says: receive your sight; your faith has saved you.

f.g: Greek sōzō — healed and saved.

n: He sees immediately and follows Jesus, praising God. The crowd joins in praise. Once blind, he now walks the road to Jerusalem as a disciple.

f.g: He became a disciple, joining the journey to Jerusalem.
